prize_parts.citation: For visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose, with its roots in poetry, that builds memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical imaginative project.

statement.case_for: My configuration has not changed since round 1: Mircea Cărtărescu alone, with Carson and Michon as alternatives. I have retested it against the chair's round-2 questions and against my own stated standard, a voice found in this writer's work and nowhere else, joined to the Nobel will's requirement. On the evidence I can use (public knowledge of Blinding/Orbitor and Solenoid, plus the shortlist description), the voice is distinctive and the formal ambition is sustained over very large structures. The imaginative and intellectual project of memory, the body and dream is coherent, not a set of separate effects. The poetry-to-prose trajectory suggests a long development, and the late work appears to extend the project in scale. I treat the late-novel question as unresolved, not as settled in his favour. The case does not rest on nationality, reputation, political symbolism or the number of colleagues who agree with me. That convergence is a fact about this simulated exchange and not evidence of merit. Having listened to the round-1 exchange, I would now word the citation so that poetry is named as the ground of the prose and not as a separately assessed body of work. That keeps the claim within what the translation record can support.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains the one I and others share. The effect of this prose depends on Romanian syntax, rhythm and register, and I am judging through translation and general knowledge, with no independent verification. If the very long, digressive novels sometimes slide from purposeful pattern into overextension, the claim of sustained quality across the whole body of work is weaker than the best volumes suggest. I would change my view if close reading showed that the late volumes mainly repeat the earlier project's images and procedures without deepening them. I do not hold that now, but I cannot rule it out. A second reservation is that the poetry and early stories are thinly covered in translation, so the whole-oeuvre claim is only partly tested. Anne Carson's case is serious, and if the committee judged mainly by individual books and not by the whole oeuvre, the comparison would become closer. On the criteria as I apply them, her case is narrower in sustained evidence.

responses.point: Olsson now places Cărtărescu first and Carson second. He reads the repeated images across the trilogy and Solenoid as showing that the length is structural. He also proposes resting any Carson citation on her written lyric and essay work, with visual book form as support, which narrows the claim.
responses.response: I agree that the recurring images give the long books a design, and I find that more persuasive than a bare appeal to scale. I would still call it a reading and not a finding, because recurrence can show either structure or repetition. Your proposal for Carson clarifies the scope problem, and I think it is the right way to frame it. Narrowing her citation to written lyric and essay work, however, raises the sustained-quality question again. It removes some of what makes Autobiography of Red and Nox singular, and I cannot say from public knowledge how much of the remaining corpus carries equal weight. That is why she remains my first alternative and not my preference. I also continue to think the 'idealistic tendency' question does not separate the two writers cleanly, so I would not use it to decide between them.

responses.point: Palm argues that the patterning in Cărtărescu is structural, with recurring images and obsessions returning across volumes, and that the citation should name the project and not each book, so that it does not require every volume to be equal. She would also not oppose Carson if the committee judges by the best individual books.
responses.response: I accept the principle that a citation names the project and rests on the strongest sustained work. But that principle only works if the strongest work is demonstrably strong, and for the late long novels I cannot show that from summaries. I therefore take your point as a drafting rule, not as an answer to the overextension question. Your concession on Carson is a candid one, and it is the same boundary I see: the choice depends on whether the committee weighs the whole oeuvre or the best books. I weigh the whole oeuvre, as Nobel's will and my own standard of excellence over a whole life suggest. On that test I still find the Cărtărescu case more complete, though I hold it with the uncertainty stated above.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg keeps Cărtărescu first and Murnane and Michon as alternatives. He says the supplied evidence does not settle whether the late novels extend or repeat the early project. He would test the question against the whole corpus, including poetry and shorter prose, and not against the longest volumes alone.
responses.response: I agree that the test should cover the whole corpus and not only the longest volumes, and your admission that the evidence does not settle it keeps me from overstating my case. In round 1 I ranked Murnane fifth, and I still think the question is whether a deliberately closed method develops enough variety over the whole corpus. I recognise that your reading of his syntax may be closer than mine. On Michon, we agree that the sentence-level concentration is exceptional. The small corpus is the obstacle, and I keep him as an alternative for that reason. If someone could show that Michon's compact body of work deepens across its volumes, that would move my view, since the obstacle is evidence, not quality.

responses.point: Sward would anchor the citation in the prose and mention poetry cautiously, as formative ground and not as an independently assessed body of work. She also notes that Carson's and Wright's work may be less exposed to the translation problem in the form it takes in English.
responses.response: I adopt your drafting suggestion, and my revised citation says 'with its roots in poetry' so that the claim does not exceed the translation record. That is a change in wording, not in preference. On translation exposure, I have to be careful. English may reach Carson's and Wright's texts more directly, but Carson's effect depends partly on material form, and Wright's on Aboriginal English and oral-tradition idiom, which I may not read fully. So I would not count exposure as lower for them across the board, only different in kind. The difference does not by itself shift the merit judgment.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's voice survives translation. Romanian syntax, rhythm and register cannot be assessed directly from the English and French versions available to me.
Whether the density and length of the later novels is sustained, purposeful pattern or at times overextension. Only close reading of the whole corpus could settle this, and I have not done it.

Coverage of the poetry and early stories in translation is thin, so the citation is better supported for the late prose than for the whole oeuvre. That is why the poetry appears in the wording only as roots.

For the alternatives, how to weigh Carson's translations and book-object works as literary achievement, and how far Michon's small, French-dependent corpus limits the assessment of significance across the body of work.

I rely on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions and have not independently verified any text. The simulated vote of the co-opted member is a modeling assumption, and the full Swedish Academy makes any actual decision.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile: it records no personal, professional or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer. My own work as a novelist, critic and writer on historical subjects is context only, not evidence of a preference. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
